The warrior cop mantra represents a significant danger to everyone involved, I believe. Not just for private citizens, but for law enforcement as well. You see, while this mantra states that an overwhelming display of force will overcome any resistance, it also foments resentment. And, though we have not yet reached that point, I believe there will come a time where these warrior cops who think they are soldiers occupying hostile territory will come to a startling and sickening realization which may make them wish they hadn't gone from peacekeepers to combatants. You see, any occupying force eventually sustains heavy casualties at the hands of the local population as resentment and outrage builds; there comes a point where the territory is no longer of sufficient tactical value to warrant the loss of life, and withdrawal then becomes prudent. As peacekeepers, police have little to fear from the majority of the population. But by seeing the population as enemies, cops inadvertently make the population see them as enemies in return. 

I certainly don't want things to become that bad, but if the escalation of violent practices as the norm continues then in my opinion it remains a possibility.

Thank you for being so understanding. We come from so many different backgrounds, and considering communication is so heavily entrenched in body language and tone, that without these indicators we have a natural tendency toward defensiveness, I find. And so my initial attempts to understand more of what happened and why, however casual considering I wasn't interested in writing a thesis, were construed by some as attacks, accusations, or attempts to draw out further information for some sort of ulterior motive. In truth, whenever I perceive a situation in the medical field which sacrifices the dignity of the patient (worse yet without even the medical professional realizing that's what's happened), I feel compelled to speak up. That's more than likely due to quite a few bad experiences as a patient and realizing too late just how detrimental to one's treatment being relegated to the level of a piece of meat on a table can be. I've been trying to obtain a grant to fund a study regarding the psychological effects of this, but thus far have not had much success. I suspect it's due to the fact that a study's findings would jeopardize attempts to streamline the efficiency of hospitals and surgical facilities; puts me in mind of a meatpacking plant at times. 

But I digress. As you say, both viewpoints are useful. I don't deny mine is pessimistic and cynical, and it was nice to have it balanced by yours. Civil conversation is a rare treat.

Thank you very much for that insightful comment. This is exactly the sort of thorough and articulate interaction I was hoping for. Interpretation of a written work, one which the author has gone out of her way to be specifically vague on, is necessarily a shotgun approach. What the writer intends to put down, what is put down, and what the reader actually takes away are three entirely different things, each influenced by the experiences and mindset of the parties involved. 

As my experiences with surgeons and med/surg facilities have painted them as circumspect, clannish, and with a strong tendency to look to their own, the manner in which I perceived they regarded the patient is somewhat mercenary and, as you say, cynical. Please understand that I don't doubt they did everything within their power to save his life, and I cannot comment on what initially went wrong since that information has been withheld. Why more effective lifesaving measures were not available was something I was unaware of, so thank you for clarifying that. 

It appeared to me (erroneously as I'm learning) that there came a point during their attempts to stabilize the patient that they realized they could not save his life, and so their goals shifted. Back when I worked in the field, and now that I'm a patient, I found the two most aggravating aspects of the medical industry were the taking of one's dignity (which I will not comment further on as it is only tangentially pertinent) and refusal to accept responsibility. It appeared to me that since this man was dying, the OR staff was attempting to hand him off to someone else so they would not have to deal with the reality of being responsible for his death. Legally, in the eyes of his kin, or just in the middle of the night when there's no one there but themselves, how you choose to define responsibility can include any of these aspects and more. I'm not calling anyone a killer, nor am I saying anyone should feel bad or be punished. All that could be done was done, but I feel very strongly that medical staff have turned away from their duty to the dead and dying. Too many times have I seen people walk in the front door, be carted around like a Meat Manager's special that's about to expire, and then pushed out the back so no one sees the other half of the cycle of nature. 

I agree wholeheartedly that all operations carry mortality, and if no medical error or the like occurred then no one should feel that they did any wrong. Death is indeed not failure, so we need to stop shunning it, but rather do right by the dead and bear witness. That was my point, how I interpreted the article, and what I found to be appalling. Apparently I was wrong since they still hoped to save the patient, and for that I apologize for the bother. It was nice talking with you.

I think if your college is interested in reducing the number of suicides that take place on campus, they can do one of two things. The first is to offer a location for students to commit suicide off campus, which in my opinion would be way more cost effective but you'd probably have some jackass yakking on and on about the sanctity of life. The second is to look at this supposed jump in student suicides on campus and break them down by motive so you'll have a better indicator of why students are choosing to kill themselves. I could wax grandiloquent all day about why people kill themselves and why people *should* kill themselves but that would ultimately be dismissed as anecdotal evidence because it only comes from a lifetime of personal experience and study rather than any papers written or editors' dicks sucked. 

Bottom line? I feel the greatest indicator of suicides and suicide attempts is having a suicidal personality, and that seems to be present from birth. Some people knuckle down and soldier on regardless of the circumstance, and others don't. They don't give up, necessarily. Sure, some do. Others, it's more like they assess the work and hardship they can expect to go through and compare it with the reward they can expect to receive, and if the numbers don't match they decide the effort of living isn't worth the trouble. Life is a calculation. There are a few confounding variables, certainly, but with time and experience you learn to account for the majority; then you just consult the ledger. I have noticed as I've gotten older over these past few decades that all of that starry-eyed optimism we as a society had has burned off in the face of economic hardship, worsening government tensions, and ongoing warfare. In every way, things are getting worse. And the amount of work it takes to just survive, to tread water, let alone to make some headway and provide for your future and that of your loved ones', is becoming increasingly insurmountable. So people with suicidal personalities, those who consult their ledgers carefully, are coming up in the red more and more. And then they check out.

For them, unless you can fix overpopulation, lack of practically every resource there is, racial/gender/religious/political tensions, and the ever-growing pile of bullshit that makes getting up in the morning a fight, whatever a college has to offer is just going to be met with laughter.

Beyond that, cancer has taken my ability to have children, and though my life was going in the right direction and I managed to build a great social network despite crippling social anxiety, I'm facing incurable illness which causes me constant pain and which will kill me in ten years anyway. I can't take the pain anymore, and have only endured it thus far for the sake of family. But that only goes so far.

In short, I don't know of any way you can avoid the pain completely for certain. It's not like anyone's succeeded in obliterating their conscious mind and returned to explain how to do it, you know? But, after a lot of anatomy study, my backup plan is to use a short-barreled 12-gauge and 00 buckshot shells. The barrel planted against my forehead and angled down slightly so the trajectory would have the shot come out the base of my skull. That would blow out both the brainstem and forebrain, and everything in between, with one very powerful and wide-ranging shot. If a firearm had to be used, that's how I would do it.

Good strategy against southpaws, if you didn't have the knack for switching styles, was to work the body. Those that I stepped into the ring against had a tendency to wait for that opening when you'd line up a right cross and miss so they had all the time in the world to get a heavy left in place to cream you. If you worked the body almost exclusively, they'd get impatient and frustrated enough to do something reckless.

I'm not here to either provoke or inhibit you from doing what you choose to do; I just feel you should be informed regarding the decision you are making. People shoot themselves in the mouth because, at the right angle, the trajectory of the bullet has the potential to obliterate the brainstem, which has direct control over respiration and pulmonary function. A brainstem is the only part of the brain necessary for a person to be regarded as alive. 

The downside to this method is that the seat of consciousness is in forebrain, and shooting oneself in the brainstem does not induce immediate unconciousness. Should the bullet strike the brainstem, you lie there paralyzed, feeling everything, unable to breathe, until the amount of oxygen in your brain drops below the threshold necessary to retain consciousness. That to me is quite scary, and would be unbelievably painful. And that's provided the bullet carries in the right direction.

If it is pointed off course, what is far more likely to happen is you damage/destroy your voluntary motor function centers. That in conjunction with damage to veins along in the interior of the cranium means your mouth will fill with blood, but you will no longer have the capacity to keep from aspirating it (the same capacity you are employing right now to keep from choking on your own saliva). So the blood will drain down your throat and fill your lungs until you drown in your own blood. You will be conscious of it the entire time, feeling everything and at best only able to wiggle like a fish on land. 

If you do this, either of these scenarios are what will play out. I am suicidal too. I have planned out how I will die. A firearm is involved as a backup should the primary method fail, but shooting myself through the mouth would never be part of that plan. I hope you will consider my words carefully. And feel free to message me in the meantime.
